_README: The Archivist's Day Log — companion to the session timeline (docs/TIMELINE_GUIDE.md). Dated true, written late: `day` is the day the log describes, never the day it was written; `whereabouts` says where the archivist actually was and is mandatory. Rendered at #/daylog/:id and linked from the event's filing hub and timeline.

daylogs.kicker: The Archivist's Day Log · Dated True, Written Late
daylogs.title: The Day the Building Obeyed
daylogs.subtitle: Where the Archivist Actually Was (the Feyward, in Chaos), What He Ate There, and One Museum He Should Have Read More Closely
daylogs.standfirst: The timeline says what the day was like out there. This page says where the archivist actually was — and it was not a desk. It was a doorway with a treant behind it, an argument settled on an exchange rate, four operatives who introduced themselves by colour, a floor that opened, and a night of research done in custody, cuffed by choice. The desk work came later, in the writing-late period, and this log finally owns up to the order of events. Dated true, written late. WAH.
daylogs.whereabouts: Not at this desk. On the fifth of Aethel — Material clock — Waluigi was in the Feyward on its stuck 922 clock, opening a door that had a treant behind it, and ending the night at a locked bathroom door — a satyr losing a fight behind it, the Mages' Guild beating on the one in front. All of that is filed where it belongs (see the doorway filing); none of it is this page.
daylogs.written: On the first night since then that the archive had a lamp, a door that locks, and the archivist in the chair, all three at once. The date of writing is deliberately not filed.
daylogs.imageCaption: The desk on the fifth of Aethel, as reconstructed — which is the only way this archive ever gets anything: lamplight, rain on the glass, five morning editions, and a song timed twice.

sections.heading: The Rules of This Page
sections.body:
Three rules, filed up top so nobody has to infer them — and one confession about the first draft of this page, which the archive shredded itself.

**One: the date at the top of this log is the day it describes, not the day it was written.** Every filing in this archive works this way — the desk dates by the event, never by the typing — and this page is the rule said out loud.

**Two: it was written late.** How late is not filed, on purpose. A log that dated its own writing would be quietly telling you how the story went — how much road was left, whether the lamp got used again — and this archive does not file endings it has not reached.

**Three: this log follows the ARCHIVIST, not the desk.** The first draft of this page opened with breakfast at the archive, the morning post, a comfortable chair. The archive read it back and shredded it, because on the fifth of Aethel the archivist was in the Feyward, and the Feyward does not serve breakfast at all. It serves a doorway with a treant behind it, an argument about glory against arithmetic, and a floor that opens. That is where this log starts.

What it is built from: my pocket book (bent, and fuller than it has ever been), the wire's outbound queue, the archive's maps and dossiers recalled from memory, the museum's visitor ledger, three newsstands' worth of weather, and the desk itself, which kept better records than its operator and has never once been chased by anything. The desk's half of the day is in here too — but in the ORDER it happened, and it happened LAST.

sections.heading: The Door, the Sleeve, and the Argument (No Breakfast Was Served)
sections.body:
I ended the last filing in a doorway and the fifth of Aethel began in the same one, because nothing about it improved in the interval. There was no morning routine to skip — the session CONTINUED, without a break, from the close of the library reclamation — and I want this page's food beat answered honestly up front, because the subtitle up there promises one. What did the archivist eat on the fifth of Aethel? NOTHING THAT IS ON RECORD. The kitchen that day was not a kitchen; it was an ARSENAL. The cook has been poisoning the overgrowth by feeding it for a week, Red's dinner went into the chest of the thing wearing Lady Aurelian's face instead of into anybody, and this archive declines to invent a sandwich on top of a session like that. The finding is that there was no breakfast, and the day ran anyway. Filed.

The door, then. I opened it because I open doors — the shame is filed elsewhere and at length — and Hjumpik's hand closed on air where my sleeve had been. Behind it: the Revel, mid-argument with itself, and a treant at FULL height, which is a phrase that means considerably more once you have stood in front of one. Hjumpik could not tell how damaged it was, because bark does not bleed where you can see it, and a treant with forty hit points left looks exactly like a treant with a hundred and forty; so he did the thing he does, which is stop assessing and start moving, and the sleeve survived, and narrowly, so did the rest of the outfit.

Then the argument the arc had been building to — glory against arithmetic, theatre against survival — with him telling me I pick my fights and me telling him what picking none of them has cost. The doorway filing has all of it, verbatim, including the four seconds before *I can't afford not to care anymore* became expensive. What this log adds is the settlement, because the rest of the day ran on it: *Put your own theatrics into it. So we don't die, and you get your theatrics.* Not agreement. An exchange rate. I have been paid in worse currencies and I will be paid in worse ones again.

And one confession, filed while we are in the neighbourhood: the first draft of THIS section put me at a bar in the basement — honey jars, a satyr barkeep, nine Goombas in cages — and the archive shredded that too, because that basement belongs to the next day's filing, assembled from Bowser's retelling, and my session had no breakfast in it at all. A day log dates true or it is nothing. The Feyward's fifth was the door, the argument, and the trees testing the walls while we had it — a knock, a long scrape, and a silence you could file a missing-persons report inside — with the Revel fighting itself somewhere in the house the whole time, in rounds nobody could stop. The honey can wait for the day it actually happened. This archive does not serve other people's sessions.

sections.heading: Why the Teaser Got Filed in Chaos (Because It Did)
sections.body:
Here is the question the reader is owed an answer to, and the first draft of this page dodged it: why would Waluigi — an archivist, a professional, a man with STANDARDS — file an abridged newspaper clipping as a review, from the middle of an active emergency, without checking it?

Because the queue does not wait, and neither does the Feyward.

The clipping had been in my pocket book for days. It arrived the way things from that world arrive, which is to say the archive has stopped asking. PROMO MARIO, said the headline, and underneath it: a portal, a farewell, a safe trip home. An ENDING. And endings get filed fast, because an ending feels like it will keep — it is the unfinished business that keeps you up, and here, finally, was business that had FINISHED.

So between one emergency and the next — crouched behind a barricade that Hjumpik had built out of furniture that used to be a door — I wrote the filing by pencil, in the field posture, and sent it up the queue. You cannot audit a newspaper while trees are testing the windows. You cannot even READ one properly. What you can do is file what it says and mark it for review, and the difference between those two acts is the difference between a good detective and a GREAT one, and on the fifth of Aethel I was, by that scale, merely good. The archive has had a word with itself. The word was in capital letters.

The correction arrived the way corrections do — later, when it was too late to be anything but expensive. PORTAL FAILED. Luigi missing. A Mario-shaped thing out of a television. The word *teaser* entered this archive's vocabulary that evening and it is not leaving.

I want one thing filed plainly beside the mistake: the charred note was already in my coat by then. Somebody had burned a note and left the ashes at my door, and that is the posture everything since has been filed in. The teaser was not laziness. It was a man handling what looked like a closed case, at speed, under fire, while carrying an open one. It was still wrong. Both of those sentences are true, and this archive is one of the only places that will hold them together.

sections.heading: The Day's Actual Business (Previously Filed, Pointedly Referenced)
sections.body:
What the desk calls the fifth of Aethel, the Feyward spent being itself. This section is a table of contents for things filed better elsewhere, plus the weather report, which is MANDATORY.

The door. I opened a door I had been told was a door, and the door had a TREANT behind it — full height, professionally angry — and Hjumpik pulled me out by the sleeve, and the sleeve survived, and so, narrowly, did the rest of the outfit. That is the doorway filing. Hjumpik's account of the save is that he pulled; my account is that I was pulled; the archive accepts both and notes that the truth has never once been located in the middle.

The trees came back, because the Feyward is made of them. A missed bomb throw. A second treant. And the first person in a week to ask, out loud, whether wood burns — a question this archive considers the single most hopeful sentence of the campaign.

Then the people who introduce themselves by colour — four Iron Legion operatives who could identify a dwarven king's champion by his sleepwear at forty paces — took Toad Lee and me as LEVERAGE, which is the Feyward's way of issuing a meeting invitation. And the sealed sanctuary, where a thing wearing a lady's face explained its entire plan, answered to the name Carnivorous, took a bowl of the cook's poisoned dinner directly in the chest, and opened the floor. All of that is filed — the doorway filing, the sanctuary record. I am not re-telling it here. I am READING it again, slowly, in a room that locks, which is the only correct way to read a floor opening.

The library, meanwhile, had been eaten by a shambling mound while Hjumpik was reading his own Waluipedia dossier — a sentence I have checked four times and it keeps being true — and was taken back over the following days. The cook's dinner makes the overgrowth wither. A guard spent twenty minutes protecting a plant with no face. There is violet fungus in a toilet. I am listing these instead of describing my feelings, because my feelings are not admissible and the fungus is.

sections.heading: The Night: Custody, Cuffs by Choice, and the Pocket Book
sections.body:
The session ends at a locked bathroom door — the dwarf at it, a satyr losing a fight he did not pick behind it, the Mages' Guild beating on the one in front, and the floor open in the room everyone had just stopped calling a room. What the transcript does not hold is what the archivist did with the rest of that night, and I will not invent it. What the record does hold is the pocket book, because the pocket book is mine.

Here is what is in it. Four special forces operatives crossed a planar boundary to collect ONE overdue contractor, identified him by his sleepwear at forty paces, and took two of his people as LEVERAGE while they were about it — cuffs, not cages, and mine were off before anybody noticed and back on by choice, which is a sentence I will be explaining to nobody, on the advice of this archive. And the question would not sit still: who sends a Colour Division after one dwarf, and what does the paper look like when they do? The archive did not have to leave the manor to start answering, because the archive already holds the ugly half. The arrangement: payments between the Iron Legion and Regency officials, documents bearing the Chancellor's own signature. The Mages' Guild's privileged access to Regency facilities — the same Guild whose failed contract the colours just collected like a household errand. Three names, one machine. The pocket book's next question wrote itself: where does a machine like that keep its money?

The maps say Yale Shores. An archivist who cannot recall his own maps in a building with no lamp deserves whatever the building does to him, so I recalled the province in full, at night, in custody, for something to do that was not listening to the satyr. Port Yale: the largest port on the western coast — seven thousand souls, a melting pot and a den of pirates and smugglers — Regency-held. Fort Yale: the Toadstool Guard's naval base, whose guns officially protect it. Smuggler's Cove: the Crimson Fleet's sea caves, moving goods past the Regency's own tariffs — the same coast, taxed by daylight and untaxed by dark, which is not a contradiction, it is a POLICY. A graveyard reef that has claimed hundreds of hulls; a lighthouse nobody has relit, haunted by a keeper who presumably gave up for the reasons the reef suggests; pearl-divers at the fishery; a crab kingdom with a foreign policy; star-fall on a ley-line beach; and one sea serpent — sole occupant of a trench the maps rate STRONGER THAN THE FORT, a census figure I find more honest than most. Rich, Guild-aligned, not militarized, no Legion garrison. That last line is the finding: the Legion does not need to stand in Yale Shores, because the Legion is PAID. The province where the money enters the kingdom is the province nobody guards, since everyone is already bought — and the Mages' Guild's own Astral Spire stands over the whole arrangement like a hat.

And the leader. The head of that machine is Chancellor Toadsworth, and his is the dossier this archive reads like a man checking a lock. The son who inherited everything: father Royal Chamberlain, then Acting Regent, then — if the journals are authentic — the man who enabled Peach's assassination and passed the secrets down with the furniture. *My son inherits what I built. He inherits the secrets with it.* Two readings, filed side by side for years: a villain perpetuating an eighty-five-year cover-up, or a victim of the wrong father; the archive has never managed to close the file, and I am not closing it in a pocket book in the dark. What the pocket book could add that night is narrower, and worse: the arrangement carries his SIGNATURE. Whichever reading is true, the son signed the machine's maintenance invoices personally. And the archive can now add the observation the Loyalists made possible: the Chancellor sits under house arrest — and the machine's paperwork stayed current without him. That is the leader's true nature, as far as this archive will file it. Not the engine. The HEIR. The trade would sail from his own western coast whether he signed it or not — and the morning after this night, paperwork arrived proving exactly that: nine Goombas in cages, shipped abroad by the Regency in exchange for weapons. That part is the Shepherd's Garden filing, and it is Bowser's session, not mine. The research that night was the question, and the coast, and the leader. The proof was the morning's ugly gift.

The night ended eventually. The pocket book went back in the coat, next to the charred note, where the archive keeps the things it is not done with.

sections.heading: The Writing-Late Period: Lamp, Lock, and the Requests
sections.body:
And then — after a stretch of Feyward time I decline to number, for reasons the clocks section owns up to — there was a night with a lamp, a door that locks, and me in the chair, all three at once. The first such night. You do not schedule that night. You INHERIT it.

This is when the desk's half of the day happened, and the first draft of this page had the gall to put it first: the records requests, the museum, the weather. In order, from the top.

I filed a records request with the Regal archives for anything catalogued under *television*. The clerk asked me to spell it, which I did, twice, and I am given to understand it has been provisionally filed under *furniture*. The request stands. The archive is patient and the archive is right. I re-read the charred note in full — properly this time, seated, unhurried, with the door locked, which is the reading it had been owed since the start. Every request that morning had already been written in its posture; I just finally had the lamp to see it by.

And the sequel had arrived by then — the CUT! account, the whole studio day: the button that made coffee, the ceiling escape, Luigi alive at the blue light, the song, the word, the empty house, the Director, the remote. Filed, amended, commentary track recorded over it, and one copy of [[song:song_plumber_man|Plumber Man]] on the desk played to the second verse for TIMING PURPOSES — three minutes forty-one seconds, timed twice, because the archive does not file a duration it has not checked. The neighbors have not complained. The neighbors have not dared.

The desk's day was a good day's work. It was simply not the DAY. The day was the door and the colours and the sound of trees, and the archive is done pretending otherwise, and the museum trip is next because it is the best part and I have earned it.

sections.heading: The Museum Trip (Writing-Late Period, Cont'd)
sections.body:
Wario keeps a private museum. This is on record — the man once produced a journal *out of* that museum, holding it flat on two palms like a waiter, while pitching unlimited wealth to a hire. Wario is away with an expedition, and has been quoted, accurately, saying that I could not keep a secret if it was stapled to my forehead. The museum's caretaker has received no such instructions about me and has me on file as *probably harmless and definitely tidy*, which is the nicest thing anyone has filed about the archive all year.

There is a shelf for the Nintendo Mania pilot. The archive took notes: a souvenir shirt, folded. A ticket stub. A soda can, empty, POLISHED. A churro stick — framed. Framed. The same newspaper clipping I had filed as a review, already hanging on his wall like a review hangs in a lobby.

And one laminated sheet, which I took for merchandise and pocketed, and which the reader can now open for themselves: [[prop:prop_nintendo_mania_call_sheet|the call sheet]].

Read it the way I should have read it standing there, with my hands in my pockets and no trees within earshot. A call sheet is not merchandise. A call sheet is a SCHEDULE. Scenes, cues, a cast list with our provincial guests on it BY NAME, a music cue for the song, an audience that is a TRACK — and one line, at the bottom, about who is allowed to say the word that stops the show.

I filed a confession as clutter. The museum was Wario keeping receipts on himself, and I walked past the receipts and complimented the frame. The great detective, ladies and gentlemen — though I will note, for the record, that I did at least POCKET the evidence, which is more than a merely good detective would have done. The sequel had already re-read my whole afternoon for me by then. It was gentler about it than this paragraph.

sections.heading: Three Newsstands and One Argument (Writing-Late Period, Concluded)
sections.body:
The timeline files the weather for all three worlds — and as of this writing it files each as a proper WIDGET, phases and icons and all, because a day's weather should be SEEN, not recited. This section files how the Material side of that was obtained, because the obtaining was the best field work the archive did all period.

The RNN bulletin gave me two lines and a shrug. Not sufficient. The archive does not file *a shrug* as conditions on a day a building obeyed a lord.

So: the WAH Media Collective keeps back-issue boxes, and the Collective owed me a favor, which is now repaid and re-owed in the other direction. Three newsstands after that. At the third there is a print vendor — a professional, a man of standards — who wanted to know, in escalating tones, why the tall purple one needed FIVE morning editions from the same Tuesday. I told him: research. He asked: into RAIN? I said yes. He looked at me the way the public has always looked at this archive, and then he took my coins, because that is the economy.

For the record, the weather on the fifth, Material world: low grey cloud all morning; a dry east wind that took the dust off the roads by midday; after dark, rain — steady, unhurried rain, the kind that makes a lamp and a door that locks feel like a POLICY DECISION.

And the studio world files its own widget, and its own finding: NO WEATHER ON RECORD. Internal conditions only — steam in one scene, sprinkler rain in the next, frost after that — and beyond the seats, through the windows, a sky that did not perform. And the third card files the Feyward, whose finding is the shortest of the three: no weather on record, because the session never once looked at the sky — the manor's weather is internal, and the day's worst of it came up through the floor. The archive can now state the weather on the day the building obeyed a lord, in three worlds, two of which have none on record. Nobody asked it to. That is what archives are FOR. WAH.

sections.heading: A Note on Clocks
sections.body:
Here is the objection, in the reader's own voice, because the reader has earned the courtesy: *the door, the hedge, the trees — and the desk dated three filings that day. When exactly did the archivist sit down?*

He did not. Not on the fifth. Not once.

The desk dated its filings by the days they DESCRIBE, which is what the desk has always done — the fifth was the day the studio world called the promo morning and the day the correction and the sequel describe, and the desk stamped them true. The ARCHIVIST, meanwhile, was in the Feyward, where it was the second of Aethel on a clock stuck at 922, or 722 if you ask the goblin, and the numbers do not reconcile, and that is the horror of the place, not a filing error.

This log was written on the first night since all of it that the archive had a lamp, a door that locks, and me in the chair, all three at once. The desk's half of the day — the requests, the museum, the newsstands, the song timed twice — happened in that writing-late period, and I have finally filed it in the order it occurred, at the END, where it belongs, after the doorway and the colours and the trees.

I am not filing when that night was. A log that dated its own writing would be telling you how the story went — how much road is left, whether the lamp got used again, whether anyone is still standing at the point where the reader stops reading — and this archive does not know those things yet, and will not pretend to. A memoir knows how it ends. This is a day log. It knows what I had for breakfast, who I had it with, and which way the trees were testing the wall.

WAH.
